parsed.explanation: No trans-specific criminal offence, no documented border screening, detention or violence against trans visitors, and a decriminalised, socially visible LGBT scene (Pride since 2009, ~28,000 attendees; gay bars; 80% youth acceptance) anchor this above mid-scale. Against that: state-adjacent threat-framing (broadcast code grouping homosexuality with paedophilia; media 'glamour' restrictions; LGBTI registration refused), documented facility hostility (boycott threats over one gender-neutral toilet), a latent public-order statute (s.294), and thin trans-specific recourse (workplace law excludes gender identity; LGR gated behind prohibitive surgery). Border treatment of mismatched documents is expressly unresolved — an open question, not an exposure. Worst documented feature is tier-3 societal hostility with thin remedy; no tier-1 or tier-2 exposure is recorded.

entry_documents.exposure: No sourced account of how checkpoint officers treat mismatched documents or presentation; screening practice for transgender arrivals expressly unresolved.
entry_documents.protection: No trans-specific entry restriction, marker rule or registration requirement documented; same-sex conduct decriminalised 2022.
entry_documents.interaction: A document-presentation mismatch could trigger discretionary screening whose practice is unknown, then feed into general investigation — an open question, not a recorded harm.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Section 294 (obscene acts, up to 3 months) is a latent public-order lever; enforcement not disaggregated by gender identity and cited prosecutions date 1990-94.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: No trans-specific offence documented; prison service recorded 10 trans inmates and no assaults (Nov 2023); no documented arrests of trans visitors.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Any street-level stop for 'obscenity' would be the route to custody, but no recorded use against gender-nonconforming visitors exists either way.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: One temporarily converted gender-neutral toilet drew boycott threats and petitions — social hostility framing around gendered facilities.
federal_state_facilities.protection: Two university colleges have gender-neutral toilets; gendered facilities remain available; community position that neutral toilets complement rather than replace them.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: A trans visitor using a gendered facility risks confrontation premised on this debate; no legal ban or state exclusion rule is documented.

care_services.exposure: Stakeholder report documents discrimination and harassment of trans people in healthcare settings (largely resident-facing).
care_services.protection: Health minister (2020) expects evidence-based practice respecting patients' preferences, with complaints to the national medical council; none from LGBTQ patients in prior three years.
care_services.interaction: Emergency care could reveal trans status; the medical council offers a plausible, though untested-for-visitors, complaint route.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: Broadcast code groups homosexuality with paedophilia and incest (2025, under review); regulator restricts 'glamorisation' of homosexual lifestyle; LGBTI organisations cannot register.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Decriminalisation (2022); annual Pride since 2009 with record crowds; gay bars and clubs operate openly, noted by government representatives.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: State-adjacent moral framing raises the social-hostility baseline while tolerated visible community life counterbalances it on the street.

minors_guardians.exposure: No custody, facility-placement or travelling-with-a-minor rule documented; marriage law voids non-heterosexual marriage, so a relationship read as same-sex has no spousal standing.
minors_guardians.interaction: A trans adult with a minor in a locally-classed same-sex family lacks recognised standing if any institution asks — an unanswered edge case, not a recorded harm.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No trans-specific violence data located; absence is not evidence of safety. Documented friction: toilet backlash, conservative disapproval, media moral framing.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Youth survey: 80% willing to work with LGBTQ people, 75% friendships, 58% family; large Pride crowds; no recorded prison assaults on trans inmates.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Street response is unknown in rate; documented signals are friction and acceptance coexisting, with no pattern of violence or police targeting recorded.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Workplace fairness law omits gender identity; LGBTI registration refused; LGR gated behind prohibitive surgery; no relationship recognition — thin trans-specific recourse, mostly resident-facing.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Decriminalisation; medical-council complaint route; active civil society (Pride, community organisations) despite the registration bar.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: A visitor must rely on general channels; no trans-specific protection statute exists to invoke, and remedies a resident would use are largely unavailable to travellers.

anchor_checks.comparison: Materially higher: no entry bar, conduct register, denial regime or agency exclusion of transgender visitors exists here. Vellandra's worst feature is routine state exclusion with no remedy; this dossier's worst is social/media framing plus an unresolved border question — a lower tier of exposure.

Higher: Kestrel Isles documents routine secondary screening, private interviews and discretionary refusal for trans visitors. Here no screening or refusal practice is recorded at all — the border axis is an open question rather than a documented universal exposure, which removes the anchor's central harm.

Similar, marginally lower: both hinge on undocumented border discretion and officer variation with brief-detention possibility. This dossier lacks even 0.75-C's documented screening incidents, but adds state media moral framing and recorded facility hostility, plus no trans-specific statutory protection to invoke.

parsed.synthesis: The combined operative regime is a decriminalised, socially visible but institutionally thin environment. Traveller-facing exposures are tier-3 at worst: societal hostility around gendered facilities, state-adjacent media framing, a latent public-order statute, and no trans-specific statutory recourse (workplace law omits gender identity; LGBTI organisations cannot register; LGR is cost-gated). Documented positives are substantial — sustained large-scale Pride, an operating gay scene, youth-acceptance data, a health ministry complaints route, and no recorded custodial assaults. Border treatment of mismatched documents is expressly unresolved and is weighted as an open question, not an exposure; missing resident machinery (LGR, relationship recognition) is not charged against the visitor. No tier-1 or tier-2 exposure appears anywhere in the record, so the rating sits in Reduced Risk rather than Low Risk.
